headline: A Collage Artist's Diagram of Cross-Cultural Religious Structure
lede: A multimedia artist known as @policefala is reclaiming authorship of an infographic she made roughly four years ago — a visual diagram synthesizing research into what she describes as a shared structure underlying diverse religious imagery. The work has kept circulating long enough that she felt the need to say: *I made this.* That lag between creation and credit is a familiar feature of how ideas move online.
body:
The tweet offers no image link that survives rendering, and the research sources retrieved no description of the diagram's contents. What can be established is that @policefala — Naomi, a collage and mixed-media artist — has built a body of work tagged with terms like *topology*, *alchemy*, and *Catholicism*, suggesting her framework draws on both esoteric traditions and more formal structural thinking. The diagram, whatever it shows, was framed as the product of research rather than intuition alone.

The intellectual tradition she is working in has a long pedigree. Since at least the mid-twentieth century, scholars of comparative religion have argued that apparently unrelated sacred traditions share deep structural features — recurring cosmological axes, threshold figures, light-as-divinity metaphors, mandala-like organizational schemas. Mircea Eliade mapped the *axis mundi* (the world-pillar connecting heaven, earth, and underworld) across dozens of cultures. Carl Jung read shared symbolic patterns as evidence of a collective unconscious. Joseph Campbell's monomyth compressed the world's hero stories into a single arc. Each was controversial in different ways; each also influenced how non-specialists think about myth and imagery.

What distinguishes a collage artist's approach from an academic one is the medium itself. A diagram — visual, grid-like, annotated — can make structural claims legible that would take pages of prose to articulate. It also travels. Screenshots of infographics circulate without captions, credit lines vanish, and the maker watches her work being reshared by strangers who have no idea where it came from. That Naomi spotted her four-year-old diagram in someone else's quote-tweet and thought to reclaim it publicly is as much a comment on attribution culture as it is on her research.

The tagging of *topology* is worth pausing on. In mathematics, topology studies properties that are preserved under continuous deformation — what stays the same when you stretch, bend, or fold a shape. Applied as a metaphor to religious iconography, it suggests that different traditions' images might be homeomorphic: distinct in surface appearance but equivalent in underlying relational structure. Whether the diagram makes this argument formally or loosely, the framing is more rigorous-sounding than most viral comparative-religion content, which may explain its staying power.

concepts.definition: The academic and artistic practice of identifying shared visual or symbolic patterns across different religious traditions — such as light imagery, circular cosmological maps, or threshold figures — without claiming those traditions are identical. Scholars like Mircea Eliade and Carl Jung pioneered influential (and contested) versions of this approach.

Latin for 'world axis': a cosmological symbol, found across many cultures, of a vertical pillar or column connecting the underworld, the earth, and the heavens. It appears as a mountain, tree, ladder, or pillar depending on the tradition. Mircea Eliade identified it as one of the most widespread structures in religious symbolism.

Borrowed from mathematics, where topology studies which properties of a shape survive deformation (stretching, bending — but not tearing or gluing). Applied loosely to cultural analysis, it asks what structural relationships remain constant even when surface forms change drastically across traditions or media.

The gradual loss of credit information as content is screenshot, reshared, or reposted across platforms. Original metadata — usernames, dates, captions — is stripped away with each generation of sharing, leaving the work effectively anonymous. Common for infographics, diagrams, and short-form art.

fact_check: The specific image referenced in the tweet was not accessible through the research sources, so its claims cannot be independently verified. The description of policefala as a multimedia collage artist with interests in alchemy and topology is drawn from publicly indexed Tumblr and Patreon metadata and is treated as reliable. Any characterization of the diagram's specific contents in this brief would be fabrication, so none has been offered.
